about: The guide's lessons (S16, S17): data the lesson runner walks the learner through, attached to an NPC. Step types: explain, model, listen, repeat, answer, do, recap (see LessonBook for the fields of each; a do step may name a noun to point the beacon at). Every step has a skip and a help path; a failed or uncertain turn moves on after the step's attempts (fail-forward, D-game-9). Lines are pre-rendered speech ids (speech/<id>.wav); phrases are rows of content/PHRASES.md; a repeat or answer step's prompt must allow the phrase's intent. S17 retired the two-step sample: this is the guide's first lesson, six short units (about eight minutes), and it starts by itself when the player first talks to her. The English thins from a phrase's second use. S26 (verbs): a lesson may carry session (the play session it unlocks in), objective (the English line that names it) and verbs (the forms it teaches: lemma, person, number, tense); a step may carry npc (the lesson moves from the villager to the shopkeeper); a do step may wait for talk_opened at an npc.

lessons.title: First words with Luna
lessons.english: Seven short units: hello, yes and no, what is this, please and thank you, I and you with three verbs, getting unstuck, and what the camp needs.
lessons.summary: You can greet, say yes and no, ask what something is, be polite, and say what you want, have and need.

steps.english: This is Luna, the guide. She teaches you Spanish one phrase at a time. Nothing here is a test. Enter goes on, H helps, K skips a step.
Luna waves and says hello.
Say hello back: “Hola” (OH-lah). Hold V to speak into the microphone, or press W to type.
steps.help: Say: Hola (OH-lah). It means hello. The letter h is silent in Spanish.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Hola. It means hello.

steps.english: Luna tells you her name. “Me llamo” means “my name is”. You only need to understand this one, not say it.
Next: yes and no. Luna holds things up and asks about them. Answer “Sí” for yes or “No” for no.
Luna holds up a log of wood and asks if it is wood. “Madera” means wood.
It is wood, so the answer is yes. Say “Sí” (SEE).
steps.help: Say: Sí (SEE). It means yes. It is written sí, with an accent; si without the accent means “if”.
steps.retry: Not quite. It is wood, so say: Sí.

steps.english: She holds up the same log and asks if it is water. It is not: answer “No”.
steps.help: Say: No. It means no.
steps.retry: Not quite. A log is not water, so say: No.

steps.english: Now ask what things are. “¿Qué es esto?” means “What is this?”. Luna points at something and names it.
Luna points at a log. Ask her: “¿Qué es esto?” (keh ehs EHS-toh).
steps.help: Say: ¿Qué es esto? It means what is this?
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: ¿Qué es esto?

steps.english: “Esto es” means “this is”. “Madera” is wood.
Luna points at some fruit. Ask again.
steps.help: Say: ¿Qué es esto?
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: ¿Qué es esto?

steps.english: “Una fruta” is “a fruit”: una means a. Madera and agua need no una, just like wood and water in English.
Luna holds up a bottle of water.
steps.help: Say: ¿Qué es esto?
steps.retry: Say: ¿Qué es esto?

steps.english: Agua is water.
She taps the bottle: botella.
Good manners. When someone offers you something, “Sí, por favor” means “yes, please”, and “Gracias” means “thank you”.
Luna offers you some fruit. “¿Quieres…?” means “do you want…?”.
You would like some. Say: “Sí, por favor” (SEE, por fah-VOR).
steps.help: Say: Sí, por favor. It means yes, please.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Sí, por favor.

steps.english: Luna nods at the berry bushes. You pick the fruit yourself.

steps.hud: Pick a fruit from a berry bush, then go back to Luna
steps.english: Press Esc to close this panel. Aim the dot at a berry bush (the arrow shows one) and hold the left mouse button to pick a fruit. Then walk back to Luna and press E.
steps.help: A berry bush is a green bush with red berries. Hold the left mouse button until the fruit drops into your bar.

steps.translation: Very good! You have a fruit.
steps.english: You have the fruit. Thank Luna: say “Gracias” (GRAH-see-ahs).
steps.help: Say: Gracias. It means thank you.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Gracias. It means thank you.

steps.english: “De nada” is the polite answer to “gracias”.

Spanish verbs change their ending for who does them. For “I” (yo) the ending is -o; for “you” (tú) it is -as or -es: “quiero” is “I want”, “quieres” is “you want”. Some verbs also change in the middle: “tienes” (you have), but “tengo” (I have). Luna asks about you; answer about yourself, with -o.
Luna asks what you want. “Quieres” is “you want”: the ending -es is for you.
You want wood. Say it: “Quiero madera” (kee-EH-roh mah-DEH-rah). “Quiero” is “I want”: the ending -o is for I.
steps.help: Say: Quiero madera. It means I want wood.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Quiero madera.
steps.personRetry: Answer about yourself: the ending -o, like “quiero”, “tengo”, “necesito”.

steps.english: Luna asks if you have a fruit: “tienes” is “you have”. You do: say “Tengo una fruta”. Tener changes in the middle: tienes, but tengo.
steps.help: Say: Tengo una fruta. It means I have a fruit. Tengo is I have; tienes is you have.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Tengo una fruta.
steps.personRetry: Answer about yourself: the ending -o, like “quiero”, “tengo”, “necesito”.

steps.english: Now she asks what you need. Answer about yourself, with the -o ending: “Necesito agua”.
steps.help: Say: Necesito agua. It means I need water.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Necesito agua.
steps.personRetry: Answer about yourself: the ending -o, like “quiero”, “tengo”, “necesito”.

steps.english: Everyone gets stuck. Three phrases help: “No sé” (I don't know), “Otra vez, por favor” (again, please) and “Más despacio, por favor” (more slowly, please). The buttons R, S and N do the same.
Luna points at something new. You don't know the word yet, so say “No sé” (noh SEH). It is never wrong.
steps.help: Say: No sé. It means I don't know.
steps.retry: Say: No sé. It means I don't know.

steps.english: When you say “No sé”, Luna tells you the answer.

steps.translation: Look. The wood is for the torch.
steps.english: Luna says something longer. Did you catch it?
Ask her to say it again: “Otra vez, por favor” (OH-trah behs, por fah-VOR). She will repeat her last line.
steps.help: Say: Otra vez, por favor. It means again, please.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Otra vez, por favor.

steps.english: Now ask for it more slowly: “Más despacio, por favor” (mahs dehs-PAH-syoh). She will say it slowly.
steps.help: Say: Más despacio, por favor. It means more slowly, please.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Más despacio, por favor.

steps.english: Luna explains what the camp needs. What does she say?
options: You need a torch and a bottle.
steps.help: “Necesitas” is “you need”. “Madera” is wood and “frutas” is fruit.
steps.retry: Not quite. Listen again: madera and frutas.

steps.english: Your list is at the top right. Hold the left mouse button on trees and bushes to collect wood and fruit, make a torch at the workbench (press E) and set it on the fire ring. The village has water.
You can already say or understand all of this.

lessons.title: Personas: he, she, we, they
lessons.english: Session 2: the verbs for he, she, you (polite), we, you all and they, with the villager and the shopkeeper.
lessons.summary: You can say what she wants and what we need or want, and you know he, she, we and they.
lessons.objective: Session 2: go to the village and talk to the villager to start the lesson “Personas”

steps.english: Session 2: more people. You know “I” (yo) and “you” (tú). Now: he or she (él, ella), we (nosotros) and they (ellos). The verb ending changes with the person. First a reminder from last time: “Quiero madera” (I want wood). The villager helps first, then you talk to the shopkeeper at the stall. Enter goes on, H helps, K skips a step.
He asks you what you want, with “tú” as Luna did. Answer about yourself.
steps.help: Say: Quiero madera. It means I want wood. Quieres is you want; quiero is I want.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Quiero madera.
steps.personRetry: Answer about yourself: the ending -o, like “quiero”, “tengo”, “necesito”.

steps.translation: Luna is the guide. She is my friend.
steps.english: The villager is talking about Luna. “Ella” is “she” and “es” is “is”.
He asks what Luna wants. “Quiere” is “he or she wants”. For he or she the ending is -e or -a (quiere, necesita), with no -s.
Say what she wants: “Ella quiere fruta” (EH-yah kee-EH-reh FROO-tah).
steps.help: Say: Ella quiere fruta. It means she wants fruit. Ella is she, so quiere ends in -e.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Ella quiere fruta.
steps.personRetry: Say it about her: the ending -e, like “quiere”, with no -s.

steps.english: Now “we”: nosotros. The ending is -amos or -emos: necesitamos (we need), queremos (we want), tenemos (we have). No -ie- for we: quiero, but queremos.
“Vamos” is “we go” (the verb ir, which does not follow the pattern). Said alone, it means “let's go”. He wants to go to the stall with you.
On the way, he asks what the two of you need. Water is on your list. Answer with “we”: “Necesitamos agua”.
steps.help: Say: Necesitamos agua. It means we need water.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Necesitamos agua.
steps.personRetry: Say it for the two of you: the ending -amos or -emos, like “necesitamos”, “queremos”.

steps.english: He points at the houses of the village. Now “they”: ellos. The ending is -an or -en: tienen (they have). What does he say?
steps.help: “Ellos” is they, and “tienen” is they have.
steps.retry: Not quite. Listen again: ellos tienen.

steps.english: “Somos” is “we are”: tú y yo (you and I) make nosotros. Somos is from ser, “to be”, which does not follow the pattern.
Where is Luna? “Está” is “is” (estar), as in “¿Dónde está el río?”. Estar is “to be” for where someone is; ser (es, somos) is for what someone is. What does he say?
steps.help: “Ella está” is she is.
steps.retry: Not quite. Listen again: ella está.

steps.hud: Walk to the stall and talk to the shopkeeper
steps.english: Press Esc to close this panel. Walk to the stall (the arrow shows it) and press E to talk to the shopkeeper.
steps.help: The stall is the one with the red and white awning in the village.

steps.english: The shopkeeper says “usted”: the polite “you”, for someone you do not know well. Its verb ends like he or she: “necesita”, “tiene”. You still answer about yourself, with the -o of “yo”: “Necesito pan” and “Tengo una botella”. Many shopkeepers say “usted” to customers; she said “tú” last time, and both are normal.
She asks what you need. Answer about yourself.
steps.help: Say: Necesito pan. It means I need bread.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Necesito pan.
steps.personRetry: Answer about yourself: the ending -o, like “quiero”, “tengo”, “necesito”.

steps.english: She asks if you have a bottle. Say you do.
steps.help: Say: Tengo una botella. It means I have a bottle.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Tengo una botella.
steps.personRetry: Answer about yourself: the ending -o, like “quiero”, “tengo”, “necesito”.

steps.english: Now she speaks to you and the villager together: “ustedes”, “you” for more than one person. In Latin America it is the only plural “you”, for friends and strangers alike. The ending is -en, like ellos: quieren.
Answer for the two of you: “Queremos pan” (keh-REH-mohs pahn).
steps.help: Say: Queremos pan. It means we want bread.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Queremos pan.
steps.personRetry: Say it for the two of you: the ending -amos or -emos, like “necesitamos”, “queremos”.

steps.english: And the people of the village? “Ellos quieren” is “they want”: -en again. What does she say?
steps.help: “Ellos quieren” is they want.
steps.retry: Not quite. Listen again: ellos quieren.

steps.english: Your new forms. querer: quiere, queremos, quieren. tener: tiene, tenemos, tienen. necesitar: necesita, necesitamos. ser: es, somos. estar: está. ir: vamos. Usted takes the he or she form; ustedes takes the they form. The book keeps them.
You can now say what she wants, what we need and what we want, and you understand he, she, you (polite), we and they.

lessons.title: Ayer y mañana: yesterday and tomorrow
lessons.english: Session 3: tomorrow with ir a and an infinitive, and a few past forms, with the villager and the shopkeeper.
lessons.summary: You can say what you are going to eat or do tomorrow, and what you ate, had or did yesterday.
lessons.objective: Session 3: go to the village and talk to the villager to start the lesson “Ayer y mañana”

steps.english: Session 3: yesterday and tomorrow. Three little words: ayer (yesterday), hoy (today) and mañana (tomorrow). First the verb ir, “to go”, and then “ir a” plus a verb, which is how you say what you are going to do. After that, a few past forms at the stall. Enter goes on, H helps, K skips a step.
“Hoy” is today. “Estamos” is “we are” (estar, for where we are); for “they are” it is “están”.
The verb ir, “to go”, does not follow the pattern. I go: voy. You go: vas. He, she, you (polite): va. We go: vamos. They, you all: van. “A” after it is “to”: voy a la tienda is “I go to the shop”.

steps.translation: Today you go to the shop.
steps.english: The villager says what you do today. Which one is it?
steps.help: “Tú vas”: vas is “you go”.
steps.retry: Not quite. Listen again: tú vas.

steps.english: Now tomorrow. Take a form of ir, then “a”, then a verb that does not change (the infinitive): voy a comer is “I am going to eat”, vamos a comer is “we are going to eat”. Not “voy a como”. “Mañana” can go in front: mañana voy a comer pan.

steps.translation: What are you going to eat tomorrow?
steps.english: He asks what you will eat tomorrow. Answer about yourself, with “voy a”: “Voy a comer pan”.
steps.help: Say: Voy a comer pan. It means I am going to eat bread.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Voy a comer pan.
steps.personRetry: Say it about yourself: “voy a”, like “voy”.
steps.tenseRetry: Tomorrow uses a form of ir, then “a”, then the infinitive: “voy a comer”, not “como” or “comí”.

steps.translation: What are we going to eat?
steps.english: Now he asks about the two of you. Answer with “vamos a”: “Vamos a comer fruta”.
steps.help: Say: Vamos a comer fruta. It means we are going to eat fruit.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Vamos a comer fruta.
steps.personRetry: Say it for the two of you: “vamos a comer”, like “vamos”.
steps.tenseRetry: Tomorrow uses a form of ir, then “a”, then the infinitive: “voy a comer”, not “como” or “comí”.

steps.translation: They are going to eat bread.
steps.english: He points at the houses. “Van a comer” is “they are going to eat”. What does he say?
options: They are going to eat bread.
We are going to eat bread.
steps.help: “Van a comer”: ir, a and an infinitive.
steps.retry: Not quite. Listen again: van a comer.

steps.hud: Walk to the stall and talk to the shopkeeper
steps.english: Press Esc to close this panel. Walk to the stall (the arrow shows it) and press E to talk to the shopkeeper. She will ask about yesterday.
steps.help: The stall is the one with the red and white awning in the village.

steps.english: Now yesterday: ayer. Something that is over uses another form, the past. A few are enough to start. I ate: comí. I went: fui. I had: tuve. You ate: comiste. You went: fuiste. You had: tuviste. With “ayer” use these, never “ayer como” or “ayer voy”.
She tells you what she ate. “Comí” is “I ate” (comer): the ending -í is for “I” and -iste is for “you”.
She asks what you ate yesterday. Answer about yourself, in the past: “Ayer comí fruta”.
steps.help: Say: Ayer comí fruta. It means yesterday I ate fruit.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Ayer comí fruta.
steps.personRetry: Say it about yourself: the ending -í, like “comí”, not “comiste”.
steps.tenseRetry: Yesterday uses the past form: “comí” (I ate), not “como” or “voy a comer”.

steps.translation: Did you go to the river yesterday?
steps.english: She asks if you went to the river. “Fuiste” is “you went”: the past of ir, which does not follow the pattern. For “I” it is “fui”.
Say that you went: “Ayer fui al río” (ah-YEHR fwee ahl REE-oh).
steps.help: Say: Ayer fui al río. It means yesterday I went to the river.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Ayer fui al río.
steps.tenseRetry: Yesterday uses the past: “fui” (I went), not “voy”.

steps.english: She asks if you had water yesterday. Say you did: “Ayer tuve agua”. “Tuve” is “I had”.
steps.help: Say: Ayer tuve agua. It means yesterday I had water.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Ayer tuve agua.
steps.tenseRetry: Yesterday uses the past: “tuve” (I had), not “tengo”.

steps.translation: Yesterday you went to the river.
steps.english: Now a form for “you”. What does she say?
options: Yesterday you went to the river.
Yesterday I went to the river.
Tomorrow you are going to the river.
steps.help: “Fuiste” is “you went”, and “ayer” is yesterday.
steps.retry: Not quite. Listen again: ayer fuiste.

steps.english: Yesterday and tomorrow side by side. “Ayer fui al río” has a past form, “I went”. “Mañana voy a ir al río” has voy a and the infinitive, “I am going to go”. The usual slip is to mix them: “mañana fui” or “ayer voy”. The game will tell you.

steps.translation: What are you going to do tomorrow?
steps.english: Last question: tomorrow. Say you are going to go to the river. Not “fui”: that was yesterday.
steps.help: Say: Mañana voy a ir al río. It means tomorrow I am going to go to the river.
steps.retry: Not quite. Say: Mañana voy a ir al río.
steps.personRetry: Say it about yourself: “voy a”, like “voy”.
steps.tenseRetry: Tomorrow uses “voy a” and the infinitive: “voy a ir”, not “fui”.

steps.english: Your new forms. ir: voy, vas, va, vamos, van. estar: estamos, están. Tomorrow: voy a comer, vamos a comer, van a comer, voy a ir. Yesterday: comí, comiste; fui, fuiste; tuve, tuviste. The book keeps them.
You can now say what you are going to eat or do tomorrow, and what you ate, had or did yesterday. Hoy is today.
